prompt: Use case: ui-mockup. Create one high-fidelity desktop web app lesson-player screen, landscape 16:10, edge-to-edge, crisp readable English UI, no device mockup or outer caption. This is a design proposal, not implementation. Product: HISTORY, an interactive history learning app. Same sample chapter in every alternative: The Silk Roads / At the crossroads, chapter 2 of 5. The attached reference contributes ONLY the Worlds identity: inky navy, rich plum, warm ivory, restrained amber controls, classical editorial lettering, luminous historical illustrations. Do not copy its three-phone layout or reuse its art as wallpaper. Preserve compact navigation: HISTORY, Chapters, bookmark, Sources, sound. Bottom controls: Previous, a five-part chapter progress indicator, Next. Narration is optional and user-paced: show Read / Listen, play/pause and seek; Next remains usable while audio plays. Visible prose must teach real history, not give instructions about the UI. No quiz, radio choices, scores, fake citations, generic card dashboard, oversized slogan, giant empty header, or essay hidden below the viewport. Generated historical imagery is visibly labeled Reconstruction; map routes schematic. Composition: a close, tactile evidence examination workspace. The main subject is an original historically inspired illustrated Sogdian merchant letter on fragile brown paper, enlarged for inspection on a dark plum conservation surface; a short discreet label says “Illustrative reconstruction · not an archival scan”. Beside it, a beautiful contemporary readable interpretation sheet titled “A network held together by people”, with two legible paragraphs: “Sogdian communities were important intermediaries in trade across Central Asia. Merchants living away from home relied on correspondence and trusted contacts to organise business.” “Surviving letters offer glimpses of those relationships. They also leave gaps: one person’s account cannot describe every trader, route or community.” Below, an integrated annotation connects a highlighted patch of the manuscript to the interpretive idea “Trust across distance”. Do NOT invent a translated historical quotation, document ID, or pretend this illustrative image is evidence. A small real-source link reads “Explore the Ancient Letters · Smithsonian”. Show zoom controls and a large readable “Image / Reading view” switch. An open narrow evidence drawer along the bottom contains two visually rich artifact thumbnails—a trade textile and a route map—with names, not generic icons. The selected letter and explanation occupy most of the viewport; a restrained “Next: What goods carried with them” action advances the narrative. This should feel like a premium digital exhibition: material detail, controlled light, legible reading and clear provenance, no scatter of decorative scraps or unrelated cards.
purpose: Lesson-player composition proposal; illustrative artwork and unverified generated map/chronology labels.
